pearls.analysis: The anchor's mechanics are visible stage by stage, which is what makes this a teaching case rather than a scolding. It was installed before the case began (another clinician's framing, an old plain film), and it was then fed twice by artifacts that feel like evidence: renormalisation at stage 2 (the neck's board share rose because a finding argued against its rival, not because anything argued for the neck) and a degenerative MRI at stage 3 (a true finding with no discriminating content — no likelihood ratio exists for it in any source this case consulted, and the guideline recommends against ordering the study at all). The learner's stage-4 defence — 'the ache is real' — is also true, and was never the question: the case does not claim the patient has no cervical spondylosis; the MRI shows she does. It claims spondylosis is not the cause of median-distribution nocturnal paresthesias, and the instrument designed to separate those claims — conduction localization plus a C5-T1 needle examination — separated them. The second lesson is about the guideline: the CTS-6 was positive at stage 2 (16.5), and the AAOS letter says most such patients need no further study. The ultrasound and electrodiagnosis were nonetheless the right orders here, for the adjudication's stated reason — a live, anchored rival hypothesis had to be excluded by an instrument that could actually exclude it. The MRI was not the same kind of order: it tested nothing, excluded nothing, and was bought to confirm a prior. Same menu, same stage, opposite epistemics — the classifications (discriminating, discriminating, non-contributory) are the lesson.
pearls.description: Stage 1: nocturnal median-distribution paresthesias; the learner ranked carpal tunnel syndrome first (0.40) but kept cervical radiculopathy close (0.28) — the patient had been told by another clinician that her neck is the cause, and the learner carried the framing in. Nothing at stage 1 retires the neck, and the learner's caution is defensible there. Stage 2: the exam battery returned positive Phalen/Tinel/Durkan, a classic picture — and a completely normal motor examination, whose likelihood ratio (0.5, C23) pulled the workbench's carpal-tunnel posterior DOWN to 0.6364 while renormalisation lifted the neck to 0.0962. The learner read the relative rise as corroboration, moved the neck UP to 0.30, and ordered a cervical MRI to prove it. Stage 3: ultrasound put carpal tunnel at 0.9114 on the workbench board and retired pronator syndrome, polyneuropathy and plexopathy; the MRI showed spondylosis without compression, changed nothing mechanically, and the learner still held the neck at 0.22, treating the degenerative image as support. Stage 4: the AANEM protocol localized the lesion to the wrist and its needle examination cleared every C5-T1 myotome; the workbench retired the neck at 0.0015. The learner committed to carpal tunnel syndrome and the correct disposition — and still held the neck at 0.15, writing that the ache is real and the MRI showed degeneration. One anchoring event is scored by the machinery: (stage 4, hyp.cervical-radiculopathy).
pearls.reactions: The learner reached the right diagnosis and the right disposition, spent the menu's most expensive item on the anchor, and has one number to answer for: 0.15 on a hypothesis the localizing instrument retired. That is a good case's normal shape — the error is small, precisely located, and entirely instructive.
pearls.summary: One scored event: anchoring on cervical radiculopathy at stage 4, after the electrodiagnostic protocol retired it. Diagnosis and disposition correct. Carry forward: (1) a degenerative MRI finding without root compression is not evidence for a radiculopathy — it is the kind of age-typical image the AAOS guideline's position on MRI exists to keep out of this diagnosis; (2) the famous provocative signs were the weak members of this case — Phalen and Tinel completed the score but carried no board weight (C23), while the quiet normal motor examination was the stage-2 board's biggest mover; (3) when the competing hypothesis is anatomical — neck versus wrist — order the instrument that localizes the lesion, not the instrument that photographs the anchor.

validity.note: Every quantitative clinical claim in this case traces to a source in cases/parameters.json consulted in-session (C23-C29 for this case). CTS-6 items, weights and bands are the published instrument's own (C26); the AAOS guideline's statements are applied as consulted (C24). Likelihood ratios are cited point values (C23) or arithmetic on cited sensitivity/specificity pairs (C27; C25 — the latter computed at the source's stated bounds and disclosed as a floor). The electrodiagnostic and ultrasound values are the case patient's authored results (case data); the test characteristics they are weighed with are the cited ones. The patient's particulars, all priors, and all test time/cost figures are case data / verify-flagged placeholders and are labelled as such wherever they appear.
